title: What are gRPC status codes — gRPC uses its own set of status codes (not HTTP status codes) such as `OK` (0), `CANCELLED` (1), `INVALID_ARGUMENT` (3), `NOT_FOUND` (5), `ALREADY_EXISTS` (6), `PERMISSION_DENIED` (7), `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` (4), `UNAVAILABLE` (14), `INTERNAL` (13), and `UNIMPLEMENTED` (12) — how do they map to HTTP codes in gRPC-Web/REST gateways, and how do you return rich error details (Google's `google.rpc.Status` with `ErrorInfo`/`BadRequest` detail messages)?
shortTitle: What are gRPC status codes, how do they map to HTTP codes, and how do you return rich error details?

s1_definition.profdef: gRPC defines its own numeric status codes, carried in the HTTP/2 trailer, that describe the outcome of an RPC independently of HTTP status codes. Examples include OK (0), CANCELLED (1), INVALID_ARGUMENT (3), DEADLINE_EXCEEDED (4), NOT_FOUND (5), ALREADY_EXISTS (6), PERMISSION_DENIED (7), UNIMPLEMENTED (12), INTERNAL (13), and UNAVAILABLE (14). When a request crosses a gRPC-Web or REST gateway, these map to HTTP status codes, for example INVALID_ARGUMENT to 400, NOT_FOUND to 404, PERMISSION_DENIED to 403, and UNAVAILABLE to 503. For machine-readable detail beyond the code and message, gRPC uses the richer error model based on `google.rpc.Status`, attaching typed detail messages such as `ErrorInfo`, `BadRequest`, or `RetryInfo`.
s1_definition.analogy: When a transfer at National Bank of India fails, the teller does not just hand back a blank rejection. gRPC status codes are like a small set of official stamp categories on the rejection slip: "wrong form" (INVALID_ARGUMENT), "account not found" (NOT_FOUND), "not allowed" (PERMISSION_DENIED), "come back later, counter busy" (UNAVAILABLE). These are the bank's own stamps, separate from the building's generic "closed" signs (HTTP codes), and when the slip is mailed to an external partner it is translated into their generic postal codes. The rich error details are the attached explanation sheet that says exactly which box on the form was wrong and what to fix.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** gRPC defines its own numeric status codes, carried in the HTTP/2 trailer, that describe the outcome of an RPC independently of HTTP status codes. Examples include OK (0), CANCELLED (1), INVALID_ARGUMENT (3), DEADLINE_EXCEEDED (4), NOT_FOUND (5), ALREADY_EXISTS (6), PERMISSION_DENIED (7), UNIMPLEMENTED (12), INTERNAL (13), and UNAVAILABLE (14). When a request crosses a gRPC-Web or REST gateway, these map to HTTP status codes, for example INVALID_ARGUMENT to 400, NOT_FOUND to 404, PERMISSION_DENIED to 403, and UNAVAILABLE to 503. For machine-readable detail beyond the code and message, gRPC uses the richer error model based on `google.rpc.Status`, attaching typed detail messages such as `ErrorInfo`, `BadRequest`, or `RetryInfo`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When a transfer at National Bank of India fails, the teller does not just hand back a blank rejection. gRPC status codes are like a small set of official stamp categories on the rejection slip: "wrong form" (INVALID_ARGUMENT), "account not found" (NOT_FOUND), "not allowed" (PERMISSION_DENIED), "come back later, counter busy" (UNAVAILABLE). These are the bank's own stamps, separate from the building's generic "closed" signs (HTTP codes), and when the slip is mailed to an external partner it is translated into their generic postal codes. The rich error details are the attached explanation sheet that says exactly which box on the form was wrong and what to fix.

**One line to remember:** gRPC has its own status codes in the trailer, gateways map them to HTTP codes, and rich errors attach typed details via google.rpc.Status so clients get both a category and actionable specifics.

sections.s2_technical:
Every gRPC call ends with a status, which is a numeric code plus an optional message, sent in the HTTP/2 trailer. OK means success. The error codes each have a precise meaning: INVALID_ARGUMENT means the client sent a bad value regardless of system state, NOT_FOUND means the entity does not exist, ALREADY_EXISTS means a create conflicts with an existing entity, PERMISSION_DENIED means the caller is authenticated but not authorized, UNAUTHENTICATED means there is no valid identity, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED means the call ran past its deadline, UNAVAILABLE means a transient outage and is typically retryable, UNIMPLEMENTED means the method is not implemented, and INTERNAL means a server bug. On the server you return a code by completing the observer with an error, for example `obs.onError(Status.NOT_FOUND.withDescription("account not found").asRuntimeException())`.

Choosing the right code matters because it drives client behavior, especially retries: UNAVAILABLE and sometimes DEADLINE_EXCEEDED are safe to retry, while INVALID_ARGUMENT and NOT_FOUND must not be retried because they will always fail. When a gRPC-Web or REST gateway sits in front, it maps the gRPC code to an HTTP status: OK to 200, INVALID_ARGUMENT to 400, UNAUTHENTICATED to 401, PERMISSION_DENIED to 403, NOT_FOUND to 404, ALREADY_EXISTS to 409, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED to 429, UNIMPLEMENTED to 501, UNAVAILABLE to 503, and INTERNAL to 500.

A plain code and message are often not enough; the client may need structured detail. The richer error model packs a `google.rpc.Status` message, which carries the code, a message, and a repeated `Any` list of detail messages, into the trailer. Standard detail types include `ErrorInfo` with a reason and a domain and key-value metadata, `BadRequest` with per-field violations, `RetryInfo` telling the client how long to wait, `QuotaFailure`, and `PreconditionFailure`. In Java the `protobuf-java-util` and the `com.google.rpc` types plus `io.grpc.protobuf.StatusProto` let you build and parse these. For example you build a `com.google.rpc.Status` with `BadRequest.FieldViolation` entries and convert it with `StatusProto.toStatusRuntimeException(status)`, and the client extracts them with `StatusProto.fromThrowable(t)`. A senior nuance: use the standard detail types rather than inventing your own, keep INTERNAL for genuine server bugs so it does not become a catch-all that hides client errors, and never leak sensitive internal messages in the description, because the client sees it.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — When a transfer fails at National Bank of India, the client needs to know not just that it failed but why, and whether to retry. A single generic failure makes the mobile app retry a hopeless request or give up on a retryable one. This is exactly what gRPC status codes solve — a precise category that tells the client how to react.

Problem 2 — For validation failures the client needs to know exactly which field was wrong so the app can highlight it, and for an insufficient-funds case it needs structured context, not a vague string. This is exactly what rich error details solve — typed BadRequest field violations and ErrorInfo metadata attached to the status.

The demo implements a transfer service that returns NOT_FOUND for a missing account, INVALID_ARGUMENT with BadRequest field violations for a non-positive amount, and FAILED_PRECONDITION with ErrorInfo for insufficient funds, and a client that reads the code and the structured details. Classes and steps: `transfer.proto`, `TransferServiceImpl` (returns codes + details), `GrpcServer`, `TransferClient` (parses details).

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build (needs grpc-protobuf + the com.google.rpc error-details types on classpath)
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run server and client
java -cp target/classes com.bank.status.GrpcServer
java -cp target/classes com.bank.status.TransferClient

# Behind a REST/gRPC-Web gateway, the code maps to HTTP:
#   INVALID_ARGUMENT→400  NOT_FOUND→404  PERMISSION_DENIED→403  UNAVAILABLE→503  INTERNAL→500
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer of Rs.5,000,000 from Rajesh (SAV2001), who only has Rs.1,000,000, to Priya (CUR3001).

Step 1 — The server parses the amount successfully and confirms it is positive, so the INVALID_ARGUMENT path with BadRequest field violations is skipped.

Step 2 — The server confirms SAV2001 exists, so the NOT_FOUND path is skipped.

Step 3 — The server sees Rajesh's Rs.1,000,000 is less than the requested Rs.5,000,000, so it builds a google.rpc.Status with code FAILED_PRECONDITION, a message, and an ErrorInfo detail carrying reason INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS and metadata with the available and requested amounts, then completes the call with that error in the HTTP/2 trailer.

Step 4 — The client catches the StatusRuntimeException, reads the code FAILED_PRECONDITION, then uses StatusProto.fromThrowable to extract the ErrorInfo and logs the reason and the available-versus-requested metadata, so the app can show a precise message instead of a generic failure. Behind a gateway this code would map to HTTP 400.

```
2026-10-26 15:25:02 [WARNING] code=FAILED_PRECONDITION msg=insufficient funds
2026-10-26 15:25:02 [INFO] reason=INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS meta={available=1000000, requested=5000000}
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  TransferClient.transfer(amount=5,000,000)
    ▼ gRPC / HTTP/2
  TransferServiceImpl.transfer(req, obs)
    ├─ amount invalid?        → INVALID_ARGUMENT + BadRequest(field=amount)   (HTTP 400)
    ├─ account missing?       → NOT_FOUND "account not found"                  (HTTP 404)
    ├─ balance < amount? YES  → FAILED_PRECONDITION + ErrorInfo                (HTTP 400)
    │     google.rpc.Status{ code, msg, details=[ErrorInfo{reason, available, requested}] }
    └─ else                   → OK + TransferResponse(COMPLETED)               (HTTP 200)
    ▼ status in HTTP/2 trailer
  TransferClient catches StatusRuntimeException
    │ e.getStatus().getCode() = FAILED_PRECONDITION
    │ StatusProto.fromThrowable(e) → unpack ErrorInfo
    ▼ app shows: "Insufficient funds: available 1,000,000, requested 5,000,000"
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — gRPC Errors Across a Gateway ═══

  ┌──────────┐ HTTP  ┌──────────────────┐  gRPC   ┌──────────────────┐ JDBC ┌────────────┐
  │ Mobile   │──────→│ REST/gRPC-Web GW │────────→│ Transfer Svc     │─────→│ PostgreSQL │
  │ App      │ 400/  │ maps code↔HTTP:  │ status  │ returns code +   │      └────────────┘
  └──────────┘ 404/  │ INVALID_ARG→400  │ + details│ google.rpc.Status│
               503   │ NOT_FOUND→404    │         └──────────────────┘
                     │ UNAVAILABLE→503  │
                     └──────────────────┘
  Retry policy keys off code: UNAVAILABLE retryable; INVALID_ARGUMENT/NOT_FOUND not.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Rich Error Model Design ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Typed Error Model: google.rpc.Status + Any detail messages     │
  │    WHY: machine-readable specifics beyond a flat string        │
  │ Builder: Status/ErrorInfo/BadRequest builders                  │
  │    WHY: assemble structured details cleanly                    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: each failure path returns one precise code + detail         │
  │ O: add a new detail type (QuotaFailure) without changing codes │
  │ I: BadRequest/ErrorInfo/RetryInfo = small focused detail types │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Code → HTTP Mapping (as prose) ────────────────────────────
  OK(0)→200  INVALID_ARGUMENT(3)→400  DEADLINE_EXCEEDED(4)→504/408
  NOT_FOUND(5)→404  ALREADY_EXISTS(6)→409  PERMISSION_DENIED(7)→403
  RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED(8)→429  UNIMPLEMENTED(12)→501  INTERNAL(13)→500
  UNAVAILABLE(14)→503  UNAUTHENTICATED(16)→401

  ── Retry Decision (as prose) ─────────────────────────────────
  retryable  : UNAVAILABLE, sometimes DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
  NOT retry  : INVALID_ARGUMENT, NOT_FOUND, PERMISSION_DENIED

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. client transfer(amount too big)
  2.   → server detects balance < amount
  3.   → build google.rpc.Status(FAILED_PRECONDITION, ErrorInfo)
  4.   → StatusProto.toStatusRuntimeException → trailer
  5.   → client StatusProto.fromThrowable → unpack ErrorInfo
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
gRPC does not use HTTP status codes; it has its own small set of numeric status codes carried in the HTTP/2 trailer at the end of every call. OK is zero, and the error codes each have a precise meaning: INVALID_ARGUMENT for a bad client value, NOT_FOUND for a missing entity, ALREADY_EXISTS for a create conflict, PERMISSION_DENIED when the caller is authenticated but not authorized, UNAUTHENTICATED when there is no valid identity, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED when the call runs past its deadline, UNAVAILABLE for a transient outage, UNIMPLEMENTED for a missing method, and INTERNAL for a genuine server bug. On the server I return one by completing the observer with the corresponding status as a runtime exception.

Picking the right code is not cosmetic, because it drives client behavior, especially retries. UNAVAILABLE is typically safe to retry, and sometimes DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, but INVALID_ARGUMENT and NOT_FOUND must never be retried because they will always fail the same way. When a gRPC-Web or REST gateway sits in front, it maps my gRPC code to an HTTP status, so INVALID_ARGUMENT becomes 400, UNAUTHENTICATED 401, PERMISSION_DENIED 403, NOT_FOUND 404, ALREADY_EXISTS 409, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED 429, UNIMPLEMENTED 501, INTERNAL 500, and UNAVAILABLE 503.

A plain code and message are often not enough, so for machine-readable specifics I use gRPC's richer error model, which packs a google.rpc.Status into the trailer carrying the code, a message, and a list of typed detail messages. The standard detail types are things like ErrorInfo with a reason, a domain, and metadata; BadRequest with per-field violations; and RetryInfo telling the client how long to wait. In Java I build these with the com.google.rpc types and convert with StatusProto.toStatusRuntimeException, and the client extracts them with StatusProto.fromThrowable.

In my banking work at National Bank of India this is exactly how the transfer service reported failures. A non-positive amount returned INVALID_ARGUMENT with a BadRequest field violation so the mobile app could highlight the exact field, a missing account returned NOT_FOUND, and an over-limit transfer returned FAILED_PRECONDITION with an ErrorInfo carrying the available and requested amounts so the app showed a precise message. The senior points I always make are to use the standard detail types rather than inventing my own, to keep INTERNAL strictly for real server bugs so it does not become a catch-all that hides client mistakes, and never to leak sensitive internal information in the description because the client can read it.
